"The article begins by painting a picture of a very different time in America, before major events like Hurricane Katrina and the election of Donald Trump. Jeffrey Eugenides, a writer, wrote a sentence back then that suggested the more you learn about your country, the more you'll find to be ashamed of. This sentiment became the central idea of one of his short stories. Now, years later, it seems that national shame might even outweigh personal shame, but Eugenides believes both remain significant. He laughingly acknowledges the difficult history of slavery and argues that these problems on a larger scale go hand in hand with personal struggles— a subtle tension present in both his personal and political reflections. It shows that even personal issues can be affected by and reflect national issues. He’s currently teaching at Princeton University. His remarks are taking place in a library. Because this building isn’t quite finished, there are little reminders of the current climate there which show that things are changing. He highlights the way things have become easier for those who previously didn’t have a place, but that there’s still a lot of work to do.

*   Essentially, the text is about how national and personal issues are intertwined, particularly focusing on feelings of shame and grappling with a country's complicated history. Eugenides's work, and his perspective, is welcome considering the many changes that have happened and continue to happen. How you’re raised with your parents will change your life. But, what you do later on in life will change your life more. To him, the state of health of America is the responsibility of many people. You might have a girlfriend, but she will not necessarily be the only influence in your life.

*   Another large theme that he touches on is the difficulty of negotiating personal life and politics, and how the problems on a national level ultimately affect people on a personal level. It emphasizes the collective nature of a nation, suggesting that national problems are just personal issues amplified. The building being incomplete is also an indication that things are not necessarily finished, and there is still work to be done."
